summary: Defines a convention for HTTP response header fields that target cache directives at specific caches or classes of caches. It also defines one such field, CDN-Cache-Control, aimed at content delivery network caches. This lets a site give different caching instructions to a CDN than to browsers.

eli5.summary: You can leave different notes for the warehouse and for the shop, so each keeps your item for different times.

questions: different cache rules for cdn and browser
how does targeted cache control work
what is a cache target list
subtitle: A convention for giving different caches, such as CDNs, their own cache instructions in separate response headers.

tldr.problem: Responses often pass through several layers of caches, and the Cache-Control header treats them mostly alike, so a site cannot easily give a CDN different instructions than it gives other caches.
tldr.mechanism: Targeted cache-control fields have the same semantics as Cache-Control but a distinct name for each class of cache. The RFC defines one, CDN-Cache-Control, and a cache uses the first valid field on its own ordered target list.
tldr.outcome: Origin servers can set a longer lifetime for a CDN than for browsers or other shared caches. CDN-Cache-Control is registered as a permanent HTTP field. The RFC warns that mixed policies can cause unintended reuse of sensitive responses.

today: RFC 9213 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2022. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Target Caches Separately
sections.content:
Modern HTTP deployments often use several layers of caching: a cache on the origin server, a caching layer in the origin's network, one or more CDNs spread across the Internet, and browser caches. Operators often want to control these separately. For example, a publisher that can invalidate a CDN's cache may be happy to give it a more generous policy while keeping other caches restricted.

The Cache-Control response header (see RFC 9111) is widely used but fairly undifferentiated. Some directives such as s-maxage target shared caches, but targeting is not available for every directive, for example stale-while-revalidate. Ad hoc mechanisms exist, but their interoperability is low. This RFC defines a standard framework for targeted cache control.
sections.eli5: A website may want the big delivery warehouse to hold a copy for a long time, but want your own browser to check back often. One note for everybody cannot say both.

sections.title: Targeted Fields and Their Syntax
sections.content:
A targeted field is a response header with the same semantics as Cache-Control but a distinct name that names its target. For example, CDN-Cache-Control: max-age=60 applies to CDNs.

Targeted fields are Dictionary Structured Fields (RFC 8941). Each member is a cache response directive. A directive with no value maps to a Boolean, a quoted-string maps to a String, and a token maps to a Token, Integer or Decimal depending on its content. So max-age is an integer, no-store is always Boolean true, and no-cache is either true or a string listing field names.

Implementations MUST NOT generate values that violate these inferred types, and SHOULD NOT consume them. Parameters on directives are ignored unless other handling is specified. If a targeted field is empty or has a parsing error, caches MUST ignore it as if it were absent. Using a plain Cache-Control parser instead of a Structured Fields parser can cause interoperability problems because error handling differs.
sections.eli5: The note has to be written in a strict format, like filling in a form. If the form is blank or messy, the cache acts as if the note was never there.

sections.title: How a Cache Picks Its Instructions
sections.content:
A cache that implements this RFC keeps a target list: an ordered list of the targeted field names it uses, from most to least applicable. It may be fixed, user configurable or generated per request. A CDN might have the list [ExampleCDN-Cache-Control, CDN-Cache-Control] so its own header overrides the generic one.

When a response has one or more fields on the list, the cache MUST pick the first, in list order, with a valid non-empty value, and MUST ignore Cache-Control and Expires in that response unless no valid value is available. This is decided per response. Fields not on the cache's list MUST NOT change its behavior and MUST be passed through.

Caches using a targeted field MUST implement max-age, must-revalidate, no-store, no-cache and private, and SHOULD implement other directives they support in Cache-Control. Precedence is the same as in Cache-Control: no-store and no-cache make max-age inoperative, and unknown extension directives are ignored.
sections.eli5: Each cache has a list of the notes it listens to, in order. It reads the first good one and ignores the general note. If none is good, it uses the general note.

sections.title: CDN-Cache-Control and Defining New Fields
sections.content:
CDN-Cache-Control is a targeted field that lets origin servers control CDN caches placed between them and clients, separately from other caches. It applies to caches that are part of a distributed network that operates on behalf of an origin server. CDN caches will typically forward it so downstream CDN caches can use it too, but they MAY remove it when that is undesirable.

A new targeted field for another class of cache can be defined by asking for registration in the HTTP Field Name Registry. By convention such fields end in -Cache-Control, such as ExampleCDN-Cache-Control, but that suffix MUST NOT be used by itself to identify a targeted field.
sections.eli5: There is one ready-made note just for delivery warehouses. If someone wants a note for another kind of helper, they can ask to add one to the official list.

sections.title: Examples and Freshness Interaction
sections.content:
With Cache-Control: max-age=60, s-maxage=120 and CDN-Cache-Control: max-age=600, a CDN considers the response fresh for 600 seconds, other shared caches for 120 seconds, and remaining caches for 60 seconds. With CDN-Cache-Control: max-age=600 and Cache-Control: no-store, the CDN keeps it for 600 seconds and all other caches must not store it. With only Cache-Control: no-store, no cache stores it. To exclude all but CDN caches, the RFC uses Cache-Control: no-store with CDN-Cache-Control: none, where none is not a registered directive and only avoids sending an empty field, which would be ignored.

Targeted lifetimes can interact badly with HTTP's single end-to-end freshness model. A response held by a CDN with Age: 1800, Cache-Control: max-age=600 and CDN-Cache-Control: max-age=3600 is fresh for the CDN but already stale for others, hurting cache efficiency. When the targeted cache has a strong coherence mechanism, deployments mitigate this by removing Age, updating Date to the current time, or updating Expires to the current time plus any max-age. The RFC places no requirement on implementations to do so.
sections.eli5: The shop might think a loaf is fresh for ten minutes while the warehouse says an hour. If the warehouse hands the loaf over after thirty minutes, the shop thinks it is already old.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of HTTP caching apply. The RFC adds that carrying several caching policies on one response can cause confusion about how it will be cached in different systems, possibly causing unintentional reuse of responses that contain sensitive information, so care must be taken.

IANA registered CDN-Cache-Control in the HTTP Field Name Registry with status permanent and the comment "Cache directives targeted at content delivery networks".
sections.eli5: If you leave several different notes, it is easy to get them muddled, and a private item might end up kept where others can see it. So be careful.
